subtitle: Journal-club style ICU update: PICO, key results, appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English.

script.heading: Intro
sentences: Welcome to Critical Care Daily for September 13, 2026.
Today we will review 3 recent ICU-relevant publications.
The format is quick listen first, then PICO, key results, critical appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English notes.
Use this as a morning triage tool, then open the source link for full-text appraisal before changing practice.

script.heading: Story 1 - Comprehensive Driving Assessment to Enable Driving Resumption
sentences: Story 1 is about Comprehensive Driving Assessment to Enable Driving Resumption in Adults Recovering From Critical Illness: A Prospective Cohort Study..
This is a cohort study from Critical care medicine.

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in Critically ill or ICU-relevant patients described in the abstract; confirm eligibility criteria in the full text., how should we interpret Exposure or intervention stated in the title/objective. compared with Comparator or control group stated in the methods/results, if present.?
We recruited 40 participants (median age, 53 yr [interquartile range (IQR), 46-64 yr]; 13 [32%] female) from six hospitals.
Twenty-six participants (79%) were assessed as capable of driving a standard vehicle; however, only 15 (45%) had resumed driving.
Seven participants (7/33, 21%) were deemed unable to drive a standard vehicle due to either physical (n = 4/7, 57%), psychological (n = 2/7, 29%), or cognitive impairment (n = 1/7, 14%).

script.heading: Story 2 - Association of Intraoperative End-Tidal CO₂, Ventilation, and
sentences: Story 2 is about Association of Intraoperative End-Tidal CO₂, Ventilation, and Hypotension With Postoperative Mortality in Noncardiac Surgery: A Retrospective Cohort Study..
This is a cohort study from Anesthesiology.

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in adults undergoing noncardiac surgery under general anesthesia with mechanical ventilation between 2010 and 2020 at a tertiary care center, how should we interpret Exposure or intervention stated in the title/objective. compared with Comparator or control group stated in the methods/results, if present.?

Among 185,455 patients (in-hospital mortality 0.85%), lower intraoperative ETco₂ was nonlinearly associated with increased mortality (adjusted odds ratio per 5-mmHg decrease from the median, 1.63; 95% CI, 1.36-1.86), independent of minute ventilation and hypotension.
No significant interaction was observed between ETco₂ and hypotension (p=0.19).
Findings were robust across sensitivity analyses.
For critical appraisal, focus on whether the design supports a causal conclusion and whether the patients resemble your ICU population.
The bedside implication is this: Useful for risk stratification and hypothesis generation, but avoid causal bedside changes unless supported by interventional evidence.
Useful English phrase: these findings should be interpreted cautiously because the details of design and applicability matter.

sentences: Story 3 is about Interpretable Machine Learning for In-Hospital Mortality Prediction in Patients With Diabetes and ARDS: Development and External Validation..
This is a recent research article from Shock (Augusta, Ga.).

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in ICU data from six Chinese institutions, how should we interpret Exposure or intervention stated in the title/objective. compared with Comparator or control group stated in the methods/results, if present.?
A total of 539 MIMIC-IV patients were divided into training and internal validation sets, and 478 patients from six Chinese centers formed the external cohort.
In-hospital mortality was 16.9%, 16.7%, and 20.3%, respectively.

script.heading: Outro
sentences: That wraps up today's journal club style update.
Before applying any finding, check the full source, the absolute effect size, and your local ICU context.
For English practice, repeat one academic phrase from each article out loud.

articles.summary: Adult ICU survivors who received mechanical ventilation (minimum 72 hr) and/or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. We recruited 40 participants (median age, 53 yr [interquartile range (IQR), 46-64 yr]; 13 [32%] female) from six hospitals. Twenty-six participants (79%) were assessed as capable of driving a standard vehicle; however, only 15 (45%) had resumed driving. Seven participants (7/33, 21%) were deemed unable to drive a standard vehicle due to either physical (n = 4/7, 57%), psychological (n = 2/7, 29%), or cognitive impairment (n = 1/7, 14%). articles.title: Association of Intraoperative End-Tidal CO₂, Ventilation, and Hypotension With Postoperative Mortality in Noncardiac Surgery: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.summary: Among 185,455 patients (in-hospital mortality 0.85%), lower intraoperative ETco₂ was nonlinearly associated with increased mortality (adjusted odds ratio per 5-mmHg decrease from the median, 1.63; 95% CI, 1.36-1.86), independent of minute ventilation and hypotension. No significant interaction was observed between ETco₂ and hypotension (p=0.19). Low intraoperative end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETco₂) has been associated with increased postoperative mortality in retrospective studies. However, whether this association is independent of intraoperative hypotension, a strong predictor of mortality, and minute ventilation, a primary determinant of ETco₂, remains uncertain. We hypothesized that low intraoperative ETco₂ is independently associated with postoperative mortality after adjustment for both intraoperative hypotension and minute ventilation.

articles.title: Interpretable Machine Learning for In-Hospital Mortality Prediction in Patients With Diabetes and ARDS: Development and External Validation.
articles.summary: Adults with diabetes and ARDS who stayed in the ICU for more than 24 hours were included. Clinical variables first recorded within 24 hours after ICU admission were candidate predictors. A total of 539 MIMIC-IV patients were divided into training and internal validation sets, and 478 patients from six Chinese centers formed the external cohort. In-hospital mortality was 16.9%, 16.7%, and 20.3%, respectively. Patients with diabetes mellitus complicated by acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) are a high-risk subgroup, but population-specific models for in-hospital mortality remain limited.
